strengths: Introduces a novel and practically important evaluation setting (end-to-end spreadsheet generation) that is underexplored relative to code/chat/table benchmarks, with a live arena and a substantial dataset (4,357 votes across 16 models) that the authors plan to release.

The analysis is unusually multi-layered: a standard Bradley-Terry leaderboard, a feature-augmented BT model that decomposes preference into 29 programmatic spreadsheet features, a data-driven failure taxonomy derived via embedding/clustering of LLM-generated loss rationales, and an independent expert rubric-based evaluation for finance-domain outputs. Together these triangulate a richer picture than a single leaderboard number.

Several findings are genuinely informative and non-obvious: substantial leaderboard compression after controlling for surface features (e.g., Claude Opus 4.5 drops 217 Elo points), domain-dependent sign reversals of the same feature (e.g., number formatting hurts in Academic/Research but helps in Finance), and distinct qualitative failure signatures across model families (Claude's losses skew toward integrity/numerical-correctness failures rather than incompleteness).

The finance expert study is a valuable sanity check on crowd preferences, showing only modest agreement (56.4% on decisive comparisons) between arena votes and domain-expert judgments, which is an important and honest finding about the limits of preference-based evaluation for specialized domains.
The task formulation, schema (SheetSpec), and match-generation algorithm are described with enough detail (with appendices) to support reproducibility of the platform mechanics.
weaknesses: Statistical reliability of the expert study is a concern: Krippendorff's alpha ranges only 0.27-0.51 across dimensions on the triply-rated subset, and 89 of 104 spreadsheets were rated by only a single evaluator, undermining confidence in the fine-grained rubric scores and their comparison to arena outcomes.

Domain-specific Bradley-Terry analyses (e.g., Table 3, 4, 13) are fit on small per-category vote subsets with 29 covariates, yet no confidence intervals, standard errors on Elo shifts, or robustness checks (e.g., bootstrap) are reported; some reported shifts are dramatic (Claude Opus 4.5 dropping 8 ranks in Academic & Research) and could plausibly reflect noise from limited sample size rather than genuine domain effects.

Model generation setups are not fully controlled: different token budgets and temperature settings across the 16 models (Table 11), and different mechanisms for schema adherence (native structured-output APIs for most providers vs. appending the schema to the system prompt for Anthropic models) introduce confounds that are not analyzed or controlled for in the preference comparisons.

The LLM-judge-based failure taxonomy, while validated against experts, only achieves 78% agreement with human-designated primary failure mode on a validation set of just 50 examples, and the multi-label tagging scheme's reliability/calibration is not otherwise quantified (e.g., no measure of judge consistency or false-positive tagging rate).

The arena relies on self-selected users and prompts (plus 436 seed prompts), with no reported analysis of voter demographics, potential vote manipulation/spam, or possible correlation among votes from the same user, which are typical caveats for arena-style studies but are not discussed here.

The core contribution is primarily an evaluation platform and observational analysis rather than a new method or model; while valuable as a benchmark/analysis paper, this bounds the technical novelty and the actionable guidance for improving models is largely deferred to future work.

The k-NN prompt-categorization pipeline used to assign submitted prompts to the 6 use-case categories is not validated (e.g., no reported classification accuracy or human spot-check), yet downstream domain-specific analyses depend critically on correct categorization.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely understudied and practically important task (end-to-end spreadsheet workbook generation), well-motivated relative to the dominance of code-generation benchmarks, with a clear articulation of why spreadsheets pose distinct structural and evaluation challenges (graph-structured formula dependencies, multi-dimensional quality criteria).

Substantial data collection effort: 4,357 pairwise votes over 16 models spanning multiple families, with a sensible Bradley-Terry/Elo pipeline grounded in established prior arena methodology (Chatbot Arena, SEAL Showdown).

The paper triangulates findings using three complementary lenses (programmatic feature regression, LLM-judged failure taxonomy, and blinded domain-expert rubric evaluation), which is a thoughtful design that surfaces genuinely interesting phenomena, e.g., substantial leaderboard compression after controlling for surface features, domain-dependent sign flips of feature effects (e.g., number formatting helping in Finance but hurting in Academic & Research), and distinct per-model failure signatures (e.g., Claude's losses skew toward integrity/numerical-correctness issues rather than spec non-compliance).

The finance expert study is a valuable reality check showing that even top arena-ranked outputs fail to meet professional modeling conventions (especially color-coding), and that crowd preference agrees with expert judgment only modestly (~56% among decisive comparisons) — an important and underappreciated point about the limits of naive preference data for specialized domains.
Good transparency in the appendix regarding prompts, schema, judge prompts, and rubrics, which aids reproducibility of the auxiliary analyses.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor of the feature-adjustment analysis is questionable: 29 features are tested with no apparent multiple-comparisons correction, several reported p-values hover near 0.05, and per-domain analyses (Tables 3, 4, 10, 13) are run on much smaller sub-samples than the full arena, yet are used to support strong claims (e.g., an 8-rank swing for Claude Opus 4.5 in Academic & Research) — the paper never reports per-domain battle counts, making it impossible to judge the reliability of these striking, headline-grabbing reversals.

The authors themselves caution that the feature-adjusted Bradley-Terry scores "should not be interpreted as an estimate of counterfactual performance," which is appropriate, but this significantly undercuts the paper's own narrative framing ("feature adjustment reveals true model quality"/leaderboard compression as an important finding) — the practical interpretability of this decomposition for readers/practitioners is left ambiguous.

The expert finance evaluation, the paper's most consequential grounding exercise, is based on only 52 battles with low inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's α 0.27–0.51 on the 15 triply-rated items); conclusions about expert/crowd misalignment are drawn despite this reliability concern not being adequately reconciled or caveated in the main text discussion.

The data-driven failure taxonomy construction is somewhat ad hoc: BERTopic-style clustering on only 260 rationales followed by manual hand-curation into 7 buckets, validated against only 50 expert-labeled examples (78% single-label agreement on a task the paper itself frames as inherently multi-label) — the taxonomy's construction and validation feel underpowered relative to the weight placed on Table 5's results.

Model configurations differ substantially in token budgets and sampling settings across providers (e.g., 16,384 vs. 2,000,000 max tokens in Table 11) without justification or sensitivity analysis, which could confound cross-model comparisons, particularly for tasks that benefit from longer context/output.

Reproducibility is compromised by the live, evolving nature of the arena: the dataset underlying the reported results is not yet released (promised "upon publication"), the match-generation algorithm is adaptive/stateful, and prompt categorization relies on a k-NN classifier over a fixed small seed set (436 prompts) whose quality/validity is not evaluated — it is unclear how stable or replicable the reported Elo rankings and feature effects would be under re-collection.

Limited discussion of selection and participation bias in who submits prompts/votes (crowd composition, incentives, possible adversarial or low-effort voting), and no ethical/data-handling discussion regarding potentially sensitive or proprietary content in user-submitted financial/business prompts.

The core methodological contribution is largely an assembly of existing techniques (Bradley-Terry/Elo, covariate-augmented BT regression, BERTopic clustering, LLM-as-judge) applied to a new domain rather than new methodology; the significance of the work rests heavily on the robustness of the empirical findings, which, as noted above, have non-trivial statistical and reliability concerns.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored but practically significant task (end-to-end spreadsheet generation), motivated well relative to the hundreds of millions of spreadsheet users versus the much smaller programmer population.

Methodologically thorough multi-layered evaluation: standard Bradley-Terry arena rankings, a feature-augmented Bradley-Terry model with 29 programmatically extracted features, a data-driven (BERTopic-style) failure taxonomy with multi-label tagging validated against human annotators, and an independent expert rubric study grounded in professional finance conventions. This triangulation is a real strength that most single-method arena papers lack.

Substantial data collection (4,357 votes, 16 models across multiple families) with sensible anchoring, vote-count thresholds before ranking, and a dynamic match-generation algorithm that balances exposure across models.

The core empirical finding—that feature adjustment substantially compresses the leaderboard and that significant predictive features differ by domain (e.g., number formatting helps in finance but hurts in academic contexts)—is a nuanced and useful contribution with implications for RLHF/DPO data curation on structured outputs.

The expert finance study is a valuable and honest reality check: it shows crowd preference agrees with domain experts only modestly (56.4% on decisive battles) and reveals systematic shortfalls (e.g., color-coding conventions) that are invisible to generic arena voting, directly supporting the paper's central thesis that preference is multi-dimensional and context-dependent.

Strong transparency/reproducibility effort: detailed appendices documenting the JSON schema, system prompts, match algorithm, full feature list and coefficients by domain, judge prompts, rubric anchors, and example outputs; stated intent to release the dataset.
weaknesses: Inter-rater reliability for the expert finance study is low (Krippendorff's α between 0.27 and 0.51), and the expert sample is small (52 battles, only 15 triply-rated), which limits confidence in the magnitude (though perhaps not the direction) of the arena-expert disagreement finding.

Model configurations differ substantially across providers in context/output token budgets (e.g., GPT-4o capped at 16,384 tokens vs. Grok 4.1 Fast at 2,000,000) and in whether structured-output APIs vs. appended schema prompting were used (e.g., Anthropic models), which could confound cross-model comparisons in ways not fully disentangled from genuine capability differences.

The data-driven failure taxonomy relies on an LLM judge (gpt-5-mini) both to generate rationales/clusters and to apply the final tags; while validated against experts for the single top category, the paper does not report what agreement would be at the multi-label level or what the correlation-corrected chance baseline is, leaving open how reliable the broader failure signature analysis (e.g., Table 5) really is.

Domain-specific feature analyses are run on much smaller subsets per category, raising concerns about multiple-comparison correction and potential overfitting of "significant" coefficients, especially for the more dramatic ranking swings reported (e.g., Claude Opus 4.5 dropping 8 ranks in Academic & Research, Table 4).

The arena relies on self-selected, mostly expert-recruited or submitted prompts and voters rather than a demographically characterized or representative pool of spreadsheet users, so external validity to the broader (non-technical) Excel user base invoked in the motivation is not directly established.

The task formulation is restricted to single-pass, non-iterative generation of a serialized JSON representation (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), which may not reflect how spreadsheets are typically built/refined in practice and could understate or mischaracterize capabilities of agentic approaches.

strengths: Introduces a novel, live arena-style benchmark for end-to-end spreadsheet generation, an understudied but high-impact domain (500M+ Excel users), with a substantial released dataset of 4,357 votes across 16 models and accompanying prompts/artifacts/code.

Employs multiple complementary and well-triangulated evaluation lenses: a feature-augmented Bradley-Terry model (29 programmatic features), a data-driven, LLM-judged failure taxonomy validated against human experts (78% agreement), and a blinded expert rubric study grounded in professional finance conventions. This triangulation strengthens the overall narrative.

Produces genuinely interesting and actionable findings: raw arena rankings compress substantially once observable features (formatting, text density, formula error rate) are controlled for, echoing known length/format biases in chat arenas but showing model-specific confounding (e.g., Claude models' apparent formatting-driven advantage); significant features vary meaningfully by domain, which has direct implications for preference-based post-training of structured-output models.

The finance expert study is a valuable and honest addition, revealing that crowd preferences only moderately align with professional modeling standards (56-66% agreement) and that even top-ranked models fail basic conventions like color coding (M=1.97/5), a nuanced and non-obvious result that goes beyond simple leaderboard reporting.

Strong transparency and reproducibility support: detailed appendices with system prompts, JSON schema specification, match-generation algorithm, full rubric anchors, per-model token/cost accounting, and category-specific coefficient tables.
weaknesses: Inter-rater reliability in the expert finance study is low (Krippendorff's alpha 0.28-0.45), which undermines confidence in the granular per-dimension expert findings, even though the aggregate patterns (e.g., weak color-coding adherence) are argued to be robust.

Domain-stratified analyses (e.g., Academic & Research category with dramatic rank swings of up to 8 positions) are based on relatively small per-category vote counts, raising concerns about the stability/statistical power of category-specific coefficient estimates, despite reported significance.

The feature-adjusted Bradley-Terry decomposition is explicitly and correctly noted as non-causal/correlational, yet several interpretive claims in the text (e.g., "Claude models seem to have formatting tendencies that happen to align with preference votes") risk being read as stronger causal statements than the methodology supports.

Limited discussion of vote quality control (e.g., spam/adversarial voting, repeat voters, user demographics) that is standard practice to address in arena-style platforms (as in Chatbot Arena or SEAL Showdown), and no reported validation of the k-NN prompt-categorization pipeline's accuracy against human labels.

The study is restricted to single-pass, non-iterative generation of a fixed JSON schema; while acknowledged as a scoping decision, this limits ecological validity relative to how spreadsheets are typically built in practice (iteratively, often with tool use), and may advantage/disadvantage certain models unevenly.

Some fragility in statistical claims: 5 of 16 "significant" features lose significance under the more conservative Benjamini-Yekutieli correction, and the paper does not fully reconcile how much this affects the qualitative conclusions drawn from Table 2 and category-specific tables.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely underexplored task formulation (holistic, end-to-end spreadsheet workbook generation) that is meaningfully distinct from existing spreadsheet benchmarks (SpreadsheetBench, SheetCopilot) which assume gold answers for narrow manipulation tasks.
Substantial empirical effort: 4,357 blind pairwise votes over 16 models, a public dataset release, and a live arena, which could be a useful community resource.

Employs multiple complementary evaluation lenses (arena Elo/Bradley-Terry, feature-adjusted BT decomposition, LLM-judged failure taxonomy validated against human annotators, and a blinded expert rubric study for finance) rather than relying on a single scalar metric, giving a richer picture of model behavior.

Several findings are interesting and plausible: substantial leaderboard compression after controlling for surface features, domain-dependent significance of features (e.g., borders/finance color conventions matter only in finance/operations), and a meaningful gap between crowd preference and finance-expert judgment (56-66% agreement).

Good transparency in reporting: cost/token accounting, full rubrics, system prompts, and schema details are provided in appendices, aiding reproducibility of the pipeline (though not necessarily of live arena results).
weaknesses: Models were run with inconsistent configurations (temperature and especially max-token budgets vary enormously across providers, e.g., Grok 4.1 Fast at 2,000,000 tokens vs. GPT-4o at 16,384 in Table 6), which is an uncontrolled confound for the core arena rankings and is not discussed or ablated.

The central framing of feature-adjustment as revealing 'bias' analogous to verbosity bias in chat arenas is not well justified: features such as pct_text, pct_fill, and more non-empty cells plausibly indicate genuinely more complete/useful spreadsheets rather than superficial preference artifacts, so the 'leaderboard compression' narrative may conflate quality with confounding and is not clearly disentangled.

Key human-validation studies are small and show weak reliability: the failure-taxonomy check uses only 50 spreadsheets across 5 annotators, and the finance expert rubric study covers only 25 battles (50 spreadsheets) with Krippendorff's alpha of only 0.28-0.45, indicating low inter-rater agreement that undercuts confidence in the specific quantitative conclusions drawn from these studies (e.g., the 56%/63.6%/66.4% expert-arena alignment figures).

Category-specific analyses (e.g., Academic & Research feature-adjusted rankings in Table 14) are based on much smaller sub-samples of an already modest overall vote count, yielding large, possibly noisy rank swings (e.g., Claude Opus 4.5 dropping 8 ranks) that are reported without adequate uncertainty quantification at the category level.

The LLM judge used for failure-mode tagging (gpt-5-mini) is both used to discover the taxonomy (via clustering its own outputs) and to apply it at scale, creating some circularity; the 78% agreement with experts is reassuring but is reported for only a single stratified sample without clear statistical treatment of multi-label tagging reliability.

The paper is dense and defers most quantitative substance to a long appendix, with the main text sometimes asserting conclusions (e.g., 'Claude models seem to have formatting tendencies that happen to align with preference votes') that are not rigorously supported by a causal or controlled analysis distinguishing genuine capability from confound.

No actionable methodological contribution toward improving spreadsheet generation (e.g., training/post-training intervention) is demonstrated; the work is purely evaluative, which somewhat limits its significance beyond providing a benchmark/dataset.

strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated benchmark (SpreadsheetArena) for a genuinely understudied and practically important task—end-to-end spreadsheet generation—filling a clear gap relative to existing spreadsheet manipulation benchmarks (SpreadsheetBench, SheetCopilot) and general chat arenas.

Substantial scale of data collection: 4,357 blind pairwise votes across 16 models from multiple families, with a sensible Bradley-Terry/Elo methodology grounded in prior arena literature (Chiang et al., Scale AI).

The feature-augmented BT model decomposition is a methodologically interesting contribution, showing leaderboard compression and clarifying how much of the ranking signal is attributable to observable, possibly superficial, spreadsheet features (formatting, text density) versus latent 'quality'.

Multiple complementary evaluation lenses (programmatic features, LLM-judge failure taxonomy validated against expert annotators at 78% agreement, and a rigorous blinded expert study with 5 raters x 50 spreadsheets) triangulate findings and substantially strengthen the evidentiary basis of the paper's central claims.

The finance-domain expert study is a valuable and honest contribution, revealing that crowd preferences diverge meaningfully from professional modeling standards (e.g., poor color-coding adherence), which has real implications for post-training with preference data on structured artifacts.
Good transparency: cost/token accounting, detailed appendices with rubrics, prompts, and schema specification support reproducibility; dataset and code release are promised.
Category-specific analyses (finance vs. academic vs. creative) convincingly show that feature importance and rankings are domain-dependent, adding nuance beyond a single aggregate leaderboard.
weaknesses: Inter-rater reliability in the expert finance study is low (Krippendorff's alpha 0.28-0.45), and expert-arena agreement is only modestly above chance (56-66%), which somewhat undercuts confidence in the fine-grained conclusions drawn from the expert rubric, though the paper is appropriately forthright about this limitation.

The feature-adjusted BT model is explicitly described as a decomposition of correlational log-odds mass rather than a causal/counterfactual estimate, but some surrounding text (e.g., 'Claude models seem to have formatting tendencies that happen to align with preference votes') risks being read as more causal than warranted; could be stated more carefully throughout.

Many statistically significant features in the large multiple-comparison setting (29 features, category-stratified) lose significance under more conservative corrections (Benjamini-Yekutieli), and some category-specific coefficients are based on fairly small per-category sample sizes, raising concerns about the robustness of domain-specific claims (e.g., Academic & Research has only 56 prompts).

The arena relies on single-pass, non-iterative JSON generation rendered deterministically; this is a reasonable and acknowledged scope limitation, but it means findings may not generalize to more realistic agentic/iterative spreadsheet-building workflows that are increasingly common in practice.

User population composition (who submits prompts/votes to a live arena) is not deeply characterized, leaving open the possibility of selection effects in both prompt distribution and voter preferences (a common issue for arena-style evaluations, but worth more discussion).

The LLM-judge failure taxonomy, while validated on a 50-example stratified sample against experts (78% agreement), is applied at scale without broader validation across categories/domains, and the taxonomy construction itself (BERTopic-style clustering plus hand-curation) introduces subjective design choices that could affect the reported failure-mode distributions.
